correctness.rationale: Partition away from null ties by the least absolute coordinate. Fixing the other k=n-1 coordinates y in the unit k-ball gives an interval of length 2 min|y_j|, because the strongest cylinder constraint omits the least coordinate. The homogeneous function m=min|y_j| has ball radial integral 1/n and Gaussian radial integral Γ(n/2)/2. Hence 2n times its ball integral equals 4/Γ(n/2) times its integral with weight exp(-|y|²) on R^k. Product integration and the layer-cake formula give the latter as π^(k/2) times the integral of erfc(t)^k. Dividing by κ_n gives the exact stated factor 2n/√π. With u=erf(t) this is E[f(U_n)] for f=exp((erf^{-1}u)^2) and U_n=1-W^(1/n) for uniform W. This coupling makes U_n strictly decrease and f strictly increases. Also 1<f(u)≤1/(1-u) for 0<u<1 by the shifted Gaussian tail, giving finite expectations and convergence to 1. At n=2 the body is the square and R_2=4/π. Writing x=√π u/2 gives erf^{-1}(u)=x+x³/3+O(x⁵), so f=1+x²+(7/6)x⁴+O(x⁶). The exact beta moments j!/[(n+1)…(n+j)] give both coefficients; restricting first to a fixed small interval gives an O(n^-6) local remainder and the tail bound gives exponentially small error on its complement. Finally min_i v_i²≤1/n, with equality for equal magnitudes, gives the claimed maximal radius and its distinct defect scale.
residual_risks: Quadrature through selected n corroborates only those cases. No assertion for unequal radii or other cylinder families.

value.rationale: Normalization by the inscribed unit ball separates the effect of increasing dimension from trivial unit-ball scaling for a natural Steinmetz family. Strict ordering and an exact leading and next contribution to volume quantify a phenomenon not visible from the maximal radius: the radius defect is of order n^-1 but the relative volume defect is of order n^-2. The beta representation explains this distinction and controls the error rather than fitting finite values.
residual_risks: The comparison is specific to all n coordinate directions with equal cylinder radii.
